name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,146

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A Roman general: one that’s riveting for the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens rather than reads, so what counts is how the words are spoken

blocks.note: something riveting grips you, so it is a gripper; said in a non-rhotic accent the ending loses its R

explanation.surface: A Roman commander so compelling that his listeners hang on every word.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken without a final R, 'a gripper' matches the general's name; 'riveting' here means gripping, not fastening metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcus Agrippa was the leading military commander under Augustus, victor at Actium.

clue.text: Two articles about Doctor Fleming, perhaps make one doubly confused?

definitions.note: describes the character rather than naming her: she is one whom a pair of twin pairs confuses

indicators.note: to be about something is to stand around it, so one piece encircles the other

blocks.note: the indefinite article A, used twice
standard abbreviation for doctor
Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a pair of words wrapped round the Bond author's title might befuddle someone twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: The pair of articles split to sit either side of the doctor and the Bond author. In The Comedy of Errors, Adriana is baffled by two sets of identical twins.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's farce Adriana is the wife repeatedly misled by both Antipholus twins and both Dromio servants, so twins double her confusion.

clue.text: One ruined by Chancery nonsense and rhetoric about estates?

definitions.text: One ruined by Chancery nonsense and rhetoric about estates?

indicators.note: turned about means moved around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: canards are false, absurd stories
taken as written

explanation.surface: A victim of the empty talk and legal flourishes of a court fighting over inheritances.
explanation.walkthrough: Chancery was the English court of equity; in Bleak House the endless Jarndyce and Jarndyce suit over estates swallows the young ward's life and hopes.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Richard Carstone stakes everything on the Jarndyce inheritance case and dies broken when costs consume the whole fortune.

clue.text: They get steamy. That’s what Mellors was after!

blocks.note: first meaning: pans that cook eggs over steaming water
second meaning: the gamekeeper in Lady Chatterley's Lover chases illegal hunters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Steamy' and Mellors both suggest the novel's notorious love scenes, but one half is kitchenware and the other is the gamekeeper's day job.
explanation.definitionFit: Egg pans heat with steam, and a gamekeeper's duty is catching men who take game unlawfully from the estate.

clue.text: A parent of Maisie who knew a princess

blocks.note: taken as written
Ida Farange is the mother in Henry James's What Maisie Knew

explanation.surface: A mother from a Henry James novel who once met royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who knew' completes the title What Maisie Knew rather than introducing the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdi's opera heroine is an Ethiopian king's daughter held as a slave in Egypt.

clue.text: A single London novelist’s the subject of an autobiography

blocks.note: a single thing is one
Will Self, novelist born in London

explanation.surface: An unmarried London writer becomes the topic of somebody's memoir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' suggests unmarried, but it is just the number; Will Self is a London-born novelist and journalist.
explanation.definitionFit: An autobiography is a life story written by its own subject, so the author writes about their own person.

clue.text: This girl’s supporting books, concealing bad ratings

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece is held within another
in a down entry a supporting piece sits underneath, so it comes after

blocks.note: Old Testament, the books of the Bible
possessive belonging to a girl
rank means foul or rotten

explanation.surface: A girl props up a stack of books that hide some poor reviews.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ratings' looks like scores or reviews, but in the navy ratings are sailors without a commission.
explanation.definitionFit: Other ranks is the British service term for enlisted personnel below officer level, the same group naval ratings belong to.

clue.text: What’s left of Manderley?

blocks.note: surface reading: the burnt ruins of the house in Rebecca
setter's reading: what is left in a will is a deceased person's property, and Manderley is a country property

explanation.walkthrough: Manderley burns at the end of Rebecca, so 'what's left' suggests ruins; it is also the word for what a dead person leaves behind.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both landed property such as a country house with grounds and the assets bequeathed after death.

clue.text: Sleuth, unnerved stumbling across island murder mystery

indicators.note: a stumbling person moves clumsily and out of order, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
I is the standard abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A shaken detective blunders onto an island where a killing has taken place.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the book itself: Poirot solves a murder at an island hotel off the Devon coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's 1941 Poirot novel is a classic whodunit, the detective genre of crime puzzles.

clue.text: They’re not still parts in The Country Wife

blocks.note: first meaning: restless people who cannot keep still
second meaning: Sir Jasper, Lady and Mrs Dainty are roles in Wycherley's comedy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not still' could suggest characters who are dead or moving on; it means restless, while the play has a whole family of that surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Restless people twitch constantly, and Wycherley's Restoration comedy gives Sir Jasper's household that surname as a comic tag.

clue.text: A play’s resonant thread involved not gold or silver

indicators.note: involved means tangled or convoluted, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: a rich voice is deep and resonant
taken as written
the bronze place, after first and second

explanation.surface: A drama's ringing line of yarn that turns out to be neither gold nor silver thread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thread' suggests embroidery to go with gold and silver, but the metals point to medal positions.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's history about the last Plantagenet king is one of his most performed dramas.

clue.text: A Dame’s range that ended too soon

indicators.note: something that ends too soon stops short, so the last letter is lost

blocks.note: an Aga is a British brand of range cooker
the word with its final letter cut

explanation.surface: A grand lady's singing voice that faded out too early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests a singer's compass, but it is the kitchen stove. With 7 Down, this points to Dame Agatha Christie.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie was made a Dame Commander in 1971, so the title fits her by name.

clue.text: Stick up for Trainspotting’s start getting offensive

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
the title's opening letter
rude means impolite or offensive

explanation.surface: Defending the opening of Irvine Welsh's novel when it turns crude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick up for' reads as one phrase meaning defend, but the definition stops at 'Stick up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To protrude is to jut out or project above a surface, the sense of sticking up.

clue.text: Old German novelist taken in by wine’s special features

indicators.note: something taken in by another is absorbed into it, so one part goes inside

blocks.note: rosé's, with the accent ignored
Thomas Mann, author of The Magic Mountain
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An early German writer fooled by a wine's distinctive qualities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' suggests being deceived; here the novelist and the abbreviation are placed together inside the pink wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman nose has a prominent high bridge, a distinctive facial feature.

clue.text: Warn a model about Mrs Beddows?

indicators.note: turned about means moved around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Cautioning a fashion model about a certain older lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Beddows is the elderly county councillor in Winifred Holtby's South Riding; the question mark marks her as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: She sits as a senior elected member of the county council, a civic office once titled alderman.

clue.text: Verses rejected based on content

indicators.note: rejected things are sent back, so the letters run backwards
content is what a thing contains, so the letters are inside the words

blocks.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Poems turned down because of what they say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like the subject matter of the verses, but it signals letters held inside the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An ode is a lyric poem of praise, so the plural is a set of poems.

clue.text: He’s tormented us, but beat a Chess Champion first

blocks.note: to tan is to thrash
Mikhail Tal, world chess champion 1960–61
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who has plagued us, but who first defeated a grandmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He's tormented us' reads as one phrase; the definition is just 'He's tormented', and 'first' puts the other two pieces before US.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Tantalus was punished forever with food and water always just out of reach.

clue.text: He tested loyalties, switching sides to non-fiction

indicators.note: the sides are left and right, so each of those letters takes the other's place

blocks.note: non-fiction deals with real events

explanation.surface: A man who probed allegiances, defecting to the camp of factual writing.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L stand for right and left; trading them puts the R at the end and the L at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's king demands public declarations of love from his three daughters before dividing his kingdom.

clue.text: Richardson’s girl topped Pasternak’s

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, removing the first letter

blocks.note: heroine of Samuel Richardson's novel Clarissa

explanation.surface: One novelist's heroine outdid another novelist's heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topped' looks like beat or surpassed; it means beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Lara in Doctor Zhivago is Larissa Antipovna, Pasternak's heroine, so the possessive stands for 'Pasternak's girl'.

clue.text: It’s not Fair Isle, Bond’s last boat raced around

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter
going around something encircles it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: final letter of the name
Noah's vessel
to hare is to run very fast
I is the standard abbreviation for isle

explanation.surface: Not a knitted Fair Isle pattern but a boat race involving 007.
explanation.walkthrough: Fair Isle sounds like a knitwear pattern or the Shetland island, but 'Fair' is the hair colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair means blond or light-coloured, so someone with brown or black locks is its opposite.

clue.text: Eliot’s ward loved to rise around noon

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means reading bottom to top, so the word runs backwards
going around something encircles it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: to adore is to love
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A novelist's young charge loved getting up late in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise around noon' paints a lazy sleeper; in a down entry rising reverses the word, and noon supplies its abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Daniel Deronda, title hero of George Eliot's last novel, is raised as the ward of Sir Hugo Mallinger.

clue.text: End cut from X-rated Shaft DVD

definitions.note: a Blu-ray is a related optical disc format rather than a DVD as such

indicators.note: cutting the end off a word drops its final letter

blocks.note: blue means smutty or pornographic
a shaft of light is a ray

explanation.surface: Censors trim the climax from an adult-rated copy of the film Shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: Shaft looks like the 1971 detective film, but it is a beam of light.
explanation.definitionFit: Blu-ray is a high-definition optical disc used for films, a successor to the DVD format.

clue.text: Ganymede’s staff with nails hammered in

indicators.note: something hammered is beaten out of shape, so the letters are knocked into a new order
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: a rod is a stick or staff
taken as written

explanation.surface: The cupbearer of the gods carries a stick studded with nails.
explanation.walkthrough: Ganymede suggests the Greek myth or Jupiter's moon, but it is the false name taken in As You Like It.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's comedy Rosalind disguises herself as a youth calling himself Ganymede in the Forest of Arden.

clue.text: Artist like Bosse: French and pricey

blocks.note: the French word for and
French for expensive

explanation.surface: A painter in the style of Bosse produces French work that is costly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' applies to both words: the conjunction and the adjective are both in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraham Bosse was a seventeenth-century French printmaker famous for his engravings and treatise on the acid-bite process.

clue.text: A Gaskell heroine shows fidelity except for one time

indicators.note: except for means leaving out, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: fidelity to facts is truth
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A novel's heroine stays faithful apart from a single lapse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits the book: Gaskell's heroine is a seduced seamstress, so 'except for one time' reads as her single fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Gaskell's 1853 novel Ruth is named after its heroine, an orphaned young seamstress.

clue.text: He compiled sagas from broken urns or lost ruins

indicators.note: something broken is smashed into fragments, so the letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An antiquarian pieced together his stories from shattered pots and vanished remains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost' looks like a second signal, but it belongs to the letters being rearranged; only 'broken' signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: The thirteenth-century Icelandic historian wrote the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, the great collection of Norse royal histories.

clue.text: Madagascan natives consent to help from pirates

blocks.note: first meaning: nocturnal lemurs found only on Madagascar
second meaning: the seafaring cry of agreement to an order, as a pirate crew gives

explanation.surface: People of Madagascar agree to accept assistance from sea raiders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natives' suggests people, but these are animals.
explanation.definitionFit: The lemur takes its name from a Malagasy word, and sailors answer a command with a doubled yes.

clue.text: Stockings removed last by Alexei’s lover. O Lord!

indicators.note: having the last removed means losing the final letter

blocks.note: hose is an old word for stockings
Anna Karenina, lover of Count Alexei Vronsky

explanation.surface: A lover in a Russian novel peels off her stockings, prompting a gasp.
explanation.walkthrough: Tolstoy's Anna is married to one Alexei and in love with another, Vronsky.
explanation.definitionFit: The cry is a Hebrew shout of praise addressed to God, used in liturgy, much like an exclamation invoking the deity.
